source_text: Sed quia frequenter intendunt illum nobis locum quo dictum sit: ego et pater unum sumus, et in hoc illos aeque facile uincemus. si enim erat, ut haeretici putant, pater Christus, oportuit dicere: ego pater unus sum. at cum ego dicit, deinde patrem infert, dicendo ego et pater, proprietatem personae suae, id est filii, a paterna auctoritate discernit atque distinguit, non tantummodo de sono nominis, sed etiam de ordine dispositae potestatis; qui potuisset dicere, ego pater, si patrem se esse meminisset. et quia dixit unum, intellegant haeretici quia non dixit unus. unum enim neutraliter positum societatis concordiam non unitatem personae sonat. unum enim non unus esse dicitur, quoniam nec ad numerum refertur, sed ad societatem alterius expromitur. denique adicit dicens, sumus, non sum, ut ostenderet per hoc quod dixit, sumus ego et pater, duas esse personas; vnum autem quod ait, ad concordiam et eandem sententiam et ad ipsam caritatis societatem pertinere, ut merito unum sit pater et filius per concordiam et per amorem et per dilectionem. et quoniam ex patre est, quicquid illud est, filius est, manente tamen distinctione, ut non sit pater ille qui filius, quia nec filius ille qui pater est. nec enim sumus addidisset, si unum se et solitarium patrem filium factum esse meminisset. Denique nouit hanc concordiae unitatem et apostolus Paulus, cum personarum tamen distinctione. nam cum ad Corinthios scriberet, ego, inquit, plantaui, Apollo rigauit, sed deus inttague neque qui plantat est quicquam, neque qui rigat, sed qui incrementum dat deus. qui autem plantat, et qui rigat, unum sunt. quis autem non intellegat alterum esse Apollo, alterum Paulum, non eundem atque ipsum Apollo pariter et Paulum? denique et diuersa uniuscuiusque sunt officia prolata: alter enim guz plantat, et alter qui rigat. hos tamen duos, non quod unus sit, sed quod unum sint, proposuit apostolus Paulus, ut alter quidem sit Apollo, alter uero Paulus, quantum ad personarum distinctionem pertinet; [quantum uero duorum una sententia est, ueritas una est, fides una est, una atque eadem religio est, unus etiam dei timor est, unum sunt, etiam si duo sint. ipsum sunt, dum ipsum sapiunt. etenim quos personae ratio inuicem diuidit, eosdem rursus inuicem religionis ratio conducit. et quamuis idem atque ipsi non sint, dum idem sentiunt, ipsum sunt; et cum duo sint, unum sunt, habentes in fide societatem, etiam si gerant in personis diuersitatem. Denique cum ad has uoces domini imperitia fuisset Iudaica commota et temere ad usque saxa succensa, ita ut discurrerent et dicerent: on te lapidamus propter bonum opus, sed propter blasphemiam, et quia tu, cum homo sis, facis te deum, distinctionem posuit dominus in ratione reddenda, quomodo se deum aut dixisset aut intellegi uellet. quem pater sanctificauit, inquit, et misit in hunc mundum, uos dicitis, quia blasphemas, quia dixi, filius dei sum? etiam hic patrem habere se dixit. filius est ergo, non pater—patrem enim confessus se fuisset, Si patrem se esse meminisset—et sanctificatum se a suo patre esse proponit. dum ergo accipit sanctificationem a patre, est, sed filius. pater enim si fuisset, sanctificationem dedisset, non accepisset. nunc autem profitendo se accepisse sanctificationem a patre, hoc ipso, quo patre se minorem accipiendo ab ipso sanctificationem probat, filium se esse, non patrem monstrauit. missum praeterea se esse dicit, ut per hanc oboedientiam, qua uenit dominus Christus missus, non pater sed filius probetur, qui misisset utique, si pater fuisset. missus autem non fuit pater, ne pater subditus alteri deo, dum mittitur, probaretur. et tamen post haec adicit, quod omnem omnino ambiguitatem dissolueret et totam controuersiam erroris exstingueret. ait enim in ultima parte sermonis: vos dicitis, guia blasphemas, quia dixt, filius dei sum? ergo si euidenter filium dominus se, non patrem, esse testatur, magnae temeritatis et ingentis est furoris exemplum contra ipsius Christi domini testimonium controuersiam diuinitatis et religionis agitare, et Christum Iesum patrem esse dicere, cum animaduertat illum non patrem se, sed filium, comprobasse.
thought_title: The Unity of the Father and the Son
pass_a_gloss: But because they frequently direct that passage to us where it was said: I and the Father are one, and in this we will easily conquer them. For if the Father was Christ, as heretics think, it was necessary to say: I, the Father, am one. But when He says 'I', then He brings in the Father, saying 'I and the Father', He distinguishes and separates the property of His person, that is, of the Son, from the paternal authority, not only in the sound of the name, but also in the order of disposed power; He who could have said 'I am the Father' if He had remembered that He is the Father. And because He said 'one', let the heretics understand that He did not say 'alone'. For 'one' placed neutrally sounds the concord of society, not the unity of person. For 'one' is not said to be 'alone', since it is not referred to number, but is expressed in relation to the society of another. Finally, He adds, saying 'we are', not 'I am', to show through this that He said 'I and the Father are', that there are two persons; but the 'one' that He says pertains to concord and the same sentiment and to the very society of charity, so that rightly the Father and the Son are one through concord and through love and through affection. And since the Son is from the Father, whatever that is, the Son is, yet the distinction remains, so that the Father is not the one who is the Son, because neither is the Son the one who is the Father. For He would not have added 'we are' if He had remembered that He is the Father alone and the Son made solitary. Finally, the Apostle Paul also knows this unity of concord, yet with a distinction of persons. For when he wrote to the Corinthians, he says: 'I planted, Apollo watered, but God gave the increase, neither is he who plants anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase.' But he who plants and he who waters are one. Who does not understand that Apollo is one and Paul is another, not the same as Apollo, but also not Paul? Finally, the different offices of each are also proclaimed: for one plants and another waters. Yet the Apostle Paul proposed these two, not because they are one, but because they are one in the sense that Apollo is one and Paul is another, as far as the distinction of persons is concerned; but as far as the sentiment of the two is one, the truth is one, the faith is one, the religion is one and the same, and the fear of God is one, they are one, even if they are two. They are one insofar as they have the same understanding. For those whom the reason of persons divides, the reason of religion again unites. And although they are not the same, yet when they have the same sentiment, they are one; and when they are two, they are one, having a society in faith, even if they bear a diversity in persons. Finally, when the Jewish ignorance was stirred up by these words of the Lord and rashly inflamed to the point of stones, so that they ran and said: 'We stone you for a good work, but for blasphemy, and because you, being a man, make yourself God', the Lord put a distinction in the reason to be given, how He said or wanted to be understood as God. 'Whom the Father sanctified and sent into this world', He says, 'you say that I blaspheme, because I said, I am the Son of God?' Here also He said that He has the Father. Therefore, He is the Son, not the Father - for He would have confessed that He is the Father if He had remembered that He is the Father. While, therefore, He receives sanctification from the Father, He is the Son. For if He were the Father, He would have given sanctification, not received it. Now, however, by professing that He received sanctification from the Father, He proves by this very fact that He is less than the Father, receiving sanctification from Him, and thus He showed that He is the Son, not the Father. Moreover, He says that He was sent, so that through this obedience, by which the Lord Christ was sent, not the Father but the Son is proved, who was sent, if He were the Father. But the Father was not sent, lest the Father be subject to another God while being sent. And yet after these things, He adds what would dissolve all ambiguity and extinguish the whole controversy of error. For He says in the last part of the sermon: 'You say that I blaspheme, because I said, I am the Son of God?' Therefore, if the Lord clearly testifies that He is the Son, not the Father, it is an example of great temerity and immense fury to stir up a controversy against the testimony of Christ the Lord, and to say that Christ Jesus is the Father, when He has shown that He is not the Father, but the Son.

choices.why: neutral placement of 'one' emphasizes concord, not unity of person
distinguishes the property of the Son's person from the paternal authority
shows the Son's reception of sanctification from the Father

pass_b_english: Opponents constantly appeal to the passage where Jesus says, "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30), thinking they have an easy victory. But if the Father were Christ, as the heretics imagine, He would have had to say, "I, the Father, am one." Instead, He first says "I," then adds "the Father," declaring "I and the Father." By doing so He distinguishes and separates the property of His own person — that is, of the Son — from the Father's authority, not only in the sound of the name but also in the order of assigned power. He could have said "I am the Father" if He had remembered that He was the Father. And because He said "one" (unum), not "alone" (unus), the heretics should understand the difference. "One" in the neuter expresses the concord of a partnership, not the unity of a single person; it does not refer to number but to a relationship with another. Finally He adds "we are" (sumus), not "I am" (sum), to show that "I and the Father are" means two persons. The word "one" points to their concord, their shared mind, and the very society of love, so that the Father and the Son are rightly one through concord, love, and affection.

Because the Son is from the Father — whatever that means — He remains the Son while the distinction stands: the Father is not the Son, nor is the Son the Father. He would not have said "we are" if He had thought of Himself as the Father alone, a solitary Son. The Apostle Paul also knows this unity of concord while maintaining a distinction of persons. Writing to the Corinthians he says, "I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. So neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but only God who gives the growth" (1 Corinthians 3:6-7). Yet "the one who plants and the one who waters are one." Who does not see that Apollos is one person and Paul another, not the same as Apollos, nor are they a single individual? Their different offices are also set forth: one plants, another waters. Still Paul presents these two as "one" — not because they are one person, but because they are one in mind: truth is one, faith is one, religion is one and the same, the fear of God is one. They are one even though they are two. They are one insofar as they think the same thing. Those whom the reality of persons divides, the reality of religion unites again. Although they are not identical, when they share the same sentiment they are one; and when they are two, they are one, having a partnership in faith even while bearing diversity in persons.

Finally, when Jewish ignorance was stirred by these words of the Lord and rashly inflamed to the point of picking up stones, so that they shouted, "We stone you not for a good work but for blasphemy, because you, a mere man, make yourself God," the Lord drew a distinction in His answer to show how He said or wished to be understood as God. "The one whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world — you say I blaspheme because I said, 'I am the Son of God'?" Here again He declares that He has a Father. Therefore He is the Son, not the Father — for He would have confessed He was the Father if He had remembered He was the Father. While He receives sanctification from the Father, He is the Son. If He were the Father He would have given sanctification, not received it. By professing that He received sanctification from the Father, He proves by that very act — accepting it from the Father as the lesser — that He is the Son, not the Father. Moreover He says He was sent, so that through this obedience, by which the Lord Christ was sent, the Son is proved, not the Father — who would certainly have been the sender if He were the Father. The Father was not sent, lest the Father be shown subject to another God by being sent. Yet after all this He adds the final words that dissolve every ambiguity and extinguish the whole controversy of error: "You say that I blaspheme because I said, 'I am the Son of God'?" If the Lord plainly testifies that He is the Son, not the Father, it is an act of great recklessness and immense fury to stir up a controversy over divinity and religion against Christ's own testimony, and to call Christ Jesus the Father, when He has demonstrated that He is not the Father but the Son.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex theological distinctions of the Latin text regarding personhood vs. concord. Scripture citations (John 10:30 and 1 Corinthians 3:6-7) are correctly identified and applied to the relevant clauses. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the Locked Latin.
